newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Coffee nations extend their quotas.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Coffee nations extend their quotas.

text.p: Coffee nations decided on Wednesday to extend a system of cartel export quotas for a year to try to lock in some of the gains from a spectacular rally in world prices.
The 14-nation Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) led by Brazil, the biggest seller, agreed to limit exports for 12 months from July 1 to 52.75 million (60 kg) bags.
This is about the same as the volume limit that they had applied under current curbs expiring on June 30. A statement said the goal was "to ensure prices remain at a level remunerative to producers".
But the exporters said they did not want high prices to kill consumer demand, so they made provision to juggle supply within their one-year limit on a seasonal basis in line with fluctuating markets.

The London coffee talks were held against a backdrop of a rally that has taken world prices for green (unroasted) beans up by 80-100 percent since January. Consumers are paying up to 50 percent more in the shops as roasters have passed on their higher costs.
Traders cite low stocks, tight supply of Latin American arabica beans and buying of coffee futures by speculative funds to explain the surprise bubble in the market.

The exporters are enjoying a windfall but worry that high prices could hurt demand. At the same time they had to consider what may happen to the market if funds suddenly bale out, as they may later this year.
Traders and analysts said that the decisions were somewhat academic now, with the market scrambling for every bean it can get and exporters disposed to ignore quotas and sell whatever they can.
But prices are likely to weaken later in the year, after the end of the upcoming frost season in Brazil.

At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York, coffee futures eased this week as fund investors already began to cash in profits. Coffee for July traded on Tuesday at around $2.45 a pound, somewhat firmer following the ACPC decision but still below recent peaks.

The now-expired May contract had hit $2.80 last week, the highest price on the exchange since June 1977. "The market reached an extremely overbought region and basically it just corrected," said Walt Spilka, a Smith Barney analyst. "It comes down now to the weather in Brazil and, outside of a frost in Brazil, everything else is discounted." Spilka said stocks of coffee had also been rising for the past week. Brokerage GNI Ltd said in a commentary that the real test of the ACPC would be not what it does now but "what it does when prices fall if the Brazilian crop survives frost damage this winter". It had already achieved a measure of success because brokers were calling it a producer cartel, not an irrelevance, GNI said.
The ACPC said in its statement that the limit on its exports under its extended quota system would be set at 52.75 million bags for the whole of the 12 months starting on July 1.
This compared with a limit for 1996/97 orginally set at 53.55 million bags but later reduced by 800,000.
"The priority of the established policy is to ensure prices remain at a level remunerative to producers, but allowing continuing growth in worldwide consumption of coffee," the ACPC said.
The ACPC said the seasonal allocations of the programme for the whole year would be decided at a later stage, to allow a more flexible and adequate flow of coffee to the market.

A technical group of six members would monitor the situation and, if any additional action was needed, it would be suggested to a full council session in September when allocations by semester would be defined. - - London Newsroom +44 171 542 7729
